header:
Date: 2026-04-29
Time: 15:00 - 15:46 PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Dr. Helen Park (Oxford CTO), Rajan Iyer (Oxford Head of Infra), Nina Gomez (Security Lead), Tom Wheeler (ML Eng), Kelsey (Oxford note taker)
Recording: yes
Artifacts shared: security-deck.pdf, benchmark-sheet.xlsx, redwood-private-overview.pdf
summary: Discovery focused on on-prem, air-gapped deployment for regulated med device data processing. Customer requirements: fully offline updates, signed model artifacts, HSM/KMS integration, RBAC/SSO via SAML, strict network egress restrictions, and deterministic maintenance windows. Discussed Redwood Private capabilities, update/patch workflows for air-gapped sites, supported hardware (A100 vs H100), and potential fallback to Dedicated/Hosted for non-sensitive workloads. Agreed next steps include sending security package, drafting PoC runbook, and scheduling an on-site benchmarking week.
topics: Air-gapped update process and model signing
Hardware constraints and recommended GPU types (A100/H100)
KMS/HSM and key management for model keys
Network isolation and allowed outbound connections
PoC scope and success criteria (latency, throughput, cost)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we can do intros quick - I'm Maya, AE on the account, with Samir and Luis from our SE team.
[00:07] Dr. Helen Park: Hi Maya, Helen here; thanks. We'll go over our constraints - short intro: Oxford MedSys works on connected infusion devices, lots of regulated PHI, so air-gapped on premise is a must.
[00:18] Rajan Iyer: Hi all, Rajan. Infrastructure lead. We run VMware clusters at edge sites, limited outbound, we'll need step-by-step for offline updates.
[00:28] Maya Chen: Got it. Before we jump in, quick agenda: 1) requirements 2) what Redwood Private can do in an air-gapped site 3) update process and signing 4) PoC scope. Sound OK?
[00:36] Nina Gomez: yes
[00:38] Samir Patel: Quick note - transcription may miss a few acronyms, apologies if names get swapped.
[00:43] Tom Wheeler: No worries.
[00:45] [01:02] Maya Chen: Helen, can you describe the primary ML workload? Latency/throughput targets?
[01:06] Dr. Helen Park: We're running device telemetry parsing and triage models, a mix of batching and real-time alerts - 200 rps at peak on a regional hub, target p99 latency under 150ms for real-time paths. Quality must be consistent; can't degrade with quantization unless we validate.
[01:20] Tom Wheeler: Also heavy use of embeddings for similarity search, large index, so memory footprint and KV cache behavior are important.
[01:28] Samir Patel: OK, so two workloads: low-latency generation/triage and embedding/indexing. For on-prem air-gapped we typically recommend pinning model versions and using our KV cache and prefix-caching to reduce tail latencies. But we need to talk hardware.
[01:40] Rajan Iyer: On hardware - procurement wants guidance. We're evaluating A100 40GB nodes vs H100 80GB. Cost is a factor but H100 gives better perf for quantized LLMs; however we have supply constraints and discrete procurement cycles.
[01:53] Luis Ortega: H100 will help for FP16/INT8 paths but A100 can work with proper quantization and kernel tuning. Also Redwood runtime supports both; you'll want a 3-node minimum for HA and KV cache distribution.
[02:05] Nina Gomez: Security - we can't allow outbound connections except to our internal update jumpbox. Does Redwood require any direct internet egress for license checks?
[02:12] Maya Chen: Short answer: no, for Private air-gapped we support fully offline deployments. Licensing can be handled via signed license files and we support on-prem license server or manual activation. We'll send the precise flow in the security deck.
[02:23] Nina Gomez: Good - what about model updates? We need cryptographic verification and a way to stage updates without touching production.
[02:29] Samir Patel: We have an offline update workflow: model bundles are signed by Redwood, you verify signatures with your local public key store (we integrate with customer KMS or HSM). For extra assurance we can provide detached signatures + checksums and a recommended staging process: test cluster -> canary -> prod. All of that is documented in the offline-update whitepaper we'll share.
[02:44] Rajan Iyer: Does that require HSM? We do have an HSM in our datacenter, would Redwood integrate?
[02:49] Luis Ortega: Yes, we support KMS/HSM integration for key storage and signing verification. The typical pattern is storing the verification key in your HSM; Redwood signs artifacts with our private signing key and you verify offline. Alternatively, you can re-sign with a customer-managed key if you require full custody.
[03:02] Dr. Helen Park: Re-signing is interesting, we often need full control for regulated deployments.
[03:06] Samir Patel: We can support both. It adds work to the PoC but it's doable.
[03:10] [04:00] Tom Wheeler: On network - will Redwood require any telemetry back to hosted console for metrics? We need audit logs but not cloud telemetry.
[04:07] Maya Chen: Redwood Private provides a self-hosted control plane option; metrics and logs can be stored locally and shipped via secure channels if you choose. For strictly air-gapped sites we provide downloadable traces and you can upload to your internal analytics offline. No mandatory telemetry to Redwood cloud.
[04:22] Nina Gomez: Audit logs retention - we have policies for 7 years for certain events. Can Redwood store and export logs in our required format?
[04:29] Samir Patel: Yes, logs are configurable; we can export in JSON/CSV and align with your SIEM ingestion. We'll capture token-level cost/latency fields but in air-gapped mode we preserve PII filtering. We'll confirm formats in the security pack.
[04:43] [06:15] Rajan Iyer: About failover - if an edge site loses power/network, can we have a fallback to Redwood Hosted? That's unlikely given rules, but curious on options.
[06:22] Maya Chen: For regulated air-gapped, fallback to Hosted is typically not allowed. However, for non-sensitive workloads you could route to Redwood Dedicated in a different tenant. We discussed routing policies earlier - you can set policy per route. For you, looks like full isolation is the requirement.
[06:39] Dr. Helen Park: Right, isolation is mandatory. Any software updates must be approved and staged.
[06:44] Samir Patel: For the PoC we suggest building the flow: 1) offline model bundle generation and signature 2) deliver via secure USB/jumpbox 3) verification and staging 4) canary perf run 5) promote. We'll provide scripts to validate signatures and checksum.
[06:58] Tom Wheeler: One operational ask - we need low-touch automation for patching because on-site ops team is small. How much automation do you provide for scheduled maintenance?
[07:05] Luis Ortega: We provide a patch manager agent that can run in offline mode - you supply the bundle and the agent applies it on a schedule, with pre/post hooks for your validation steps. If you need full automation we'll partner with your ops to map approvals.
[07:17] [08:30] Nina Gomez: Compliance: we need evidence for SOC2 and ISO 27001, plus proof of vulnerability scanning on the images. Does Redwood scan images before delivery?
[08:38] Maya Chen: Yes, for Private deployments we run build pipelines with SBOMs and vulnerability scans. We can provide the SBOMs and scan results as part of the package. For air-gapped sites we can deliver scanned images and the SBOMs.
[08:50] Nina Gomez: And SSO/SAML? We want integration with our Okta tenant and RBAC mapped to AD groups.
[08:56] Samir Patel: Supported - SAML SSO for console access and roles can be synced from your IdP. We also support fine-grained RBAC for route-level permissions.
[09:04] Rajan Iyer: Storage - will models and KV caches live on local NVMe? We have constraints on storage encryption.
[09:09] Luis Ortega: Models are stored encrypted at rest; you can provide the encryption key or use our integration with your KMS/HSM. KV cache can be on fast NVMe; recommended to use local SSDs for low p99 latency.
[09:20] Tom Wheeler: For embeddings index - any recommendations for sharding across nodes?
[09:23] Samir Patel: Depends on dataset size; we usually shard embeddings by prefix and keep the nearest-neighbor index distributed. For your scale, a 3-node cluster with 1TB SSD each should be a starting point; we'll tailor after we run sample benchmarks.
[09:34] [11:00] Dr. Helen Park: Can you do an onsite benchmark with our sample traces? We'll want to compare A100 vs H100 and quantized 8-bit models against FP16.
[11:06] Maya Chen: Yes - recommended PoC: 1) bring sample traces and prompt sets 2) run throughput and p99 tests 3) run quality regression tests for quantized models 4) document cost/perf tradeoffs. We'll need access to your lab hardware or provide cloud-simulated nodes if needed.
[11:20] Rajan Iyer: Procurement: estimated budget window next quarter; need a firm number for 3-node cluster license + support.
[11:26] Maya Chen: We'll provide a preliminary estimate, will include options for Dedicated if you want reserved capacity instead of full on-prem, but given regulatory constraints Private on-prem is likely.
[11:36] [13:00] Nina Gomez: Regarding legal - we need to review data processing agreements and liability language for model outputs. Any redwood standard docs?
[13:06] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll share our standard DPA and customer terms; legal can redline. For model output liability we have enterprise-level terms and indemnities set per contract.
[13:15] Tom Wheeler: One practical - how are GPU drivers and CUDA handled in an air-gapped install? We have strict change controls and can't allow internet pulls.
[13:22] Luis Ortega: We'll provide tested driver bundles (NVIDIA driver, CUDA, cuDNN) as part of the offline image. You can validate in staging and then push to prod. The runtime is packaged with pinned kernel versions; we document exact versions required.
[13:34] Rajan Iyer: Great. Also need clarity on support SLAs - do you offer 24/7 for on-prem?
[13:39] Maya Chen: We have support tiers; enterprise support (included for Private customers on top tier) can be 24/7 with on-call SEs. We'll outline response and escalation in the next packet.
[13:52] [18:00] Dr. Helen Park: Success criteria for PoC: 1) hit p99 <150ms on real-time route at 200rps 2) embedding latency and recall within 2% of baseline 3) offline update process completes under our QA window and meets signature requirements.
[18:11] Samir Patel: We'll codify those in the PoC runbook.
[18:15] Maya Chen: Questions from our side: what's your timeline and who will be the technical owner?
[18:19] Rajan Iyer: Timeline - procurement cycle closes mid-June; would like PoC in late May if possible. Technical owner will be Tom with Nina as security owner.
[18:28] Maya Chen: OK, we'll aim to schedule week of May 19 for benchmarking as tentative.
[18:33] [21:00] Kelsey: (note) - Tina spelled a name incorrectly earlier.
[21:05] Tom Wheeler: small thing - are there recommended quantization profiles you support out-of-box?
[21:10] Luis Ortega: We ship recommended quantization profiles for common open models; we also provide eval harnesses to validate quality regressions on your prompts. For highly regulated outputs we recommend conservative quantization and manual evaluation.
[21:24] Nina Gomez: Is there any live demo we can see of the offline update flow?
[21:29] Samir Patel: We can record a demo and also do a live demo during the PoC kickoff. We'll share a short demo video in the security packet.
[21:36] [28:00] Dr. Helen Park: Anything else on risk? We worry about model poisoning from third-party models.
[28:07] Maya Chen: Mitigation - signed artifacts, SBOMs, vulnerability scans, and the option to re-sign with customer-managed keys. Also we can run regression tests and adversarial checks as part of the PoC.
[28:20] Rajan Iyer: For the edge sites, power is limited - what's the minimum footprint?
[28:24] Luis Ortega: Minimum recommended is a 2-3 GPU node depending on workload; for strict power constraints we can explore lower-TDP GPUs but you'll trade throughput. We'll run sizing tests during PoC.
[28:37] [35:00] Maya Chen: Recap / next steps: we'll send security-deck, offline-update whitepaper, and benchmark-sheet; Samir will draft PoC runbook; pricing and 3-node estimate in 48 hours. Can we get procurement and security owners to review by next week?
[35:14] Nina Gomez: I'll review quickly, but will need the SOC2 docs first.
[35:18] Rajan Iyer: I'll confirm procurement dates.
[35:22] Maya Chen: Perfect. Any final questions?
[35:27] Dr. Helen Park: No, thanks - appreciate the thoroughness.
[35:30] Tom Wheeler: Thanks everyone.
[35:33] [46:00] End of recording

Notes: occasional transcription errors present (names and acronyms), references to artifacts: security-deck.pdf and benchmark-sheet.xlsx (links provided after meeting).
